bio.en: Eeke de Milliano is the head of product at Retool and was one of Stripe's earliest product managers, where she helped build foundational products like Stripe Checkout, Connect, Radar, and Chargeback Protection.
bio.zh: Eeke de Milliano 是 Retool 的产品负责人，也是 Stripe 最早的产品经理之一，曾参与打造 Stripe Checkout、Connect、Radar 和 Chargeback Protection 等基础产品。

summary.en: Eeke frames process as inherently variance-reducing—useful for lifting the average but often dragging down the highest performers—and explains how the right amount of process changes by company stage. She digs into what made Stripe's internal culture so uniquely innovative and how to foster and protect innovation as an organization grows. She also shares her approach to building a 'talent portfolio'—intentionally composing a team with complementary strengths rather than hiring clones.
summary.zh: Eeke 将流程本质视为“降低方差”——它能拉高平均水平，却常常拖累最优秀的人才，并解释了流程的恰当程度如何随公司阶段而变化。她深入剖析了 Stripe 内部文化为何如此独特且具创新性，以及组织壮大时如何培养和保护创新。她还分享了打造“人才组合”的方法——有意识地把优势互补的人组合成团队，而非招一批同质化的人。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Process, by definition, is variance reducing. You're introducing it, because you worry that the variance in your org is too high. You want people to sort of meet a certain standard.
turns.zh: 根据定义，过程是减少方差的过程。您之所以引入它，是因为您担心组织中的差异太大。你希望人们达到一定的标准。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And the cost of that is obviously, while you are reducing the standard and bringing folks up to the average, you're also bringing other folks down to the average. And oftentimes, the folks you're bringing down are your highest performers, your most creative thinkers. The folks who, I think actually don't really need process to do their best work.
turns.zh: 这样做的代价显然是，当你降低标准并使人们达到平均水平时，你也将其他人降低到平均水平。通常，你打倒的人是你表现最好的人、你最有创造力的思想家。我认为这些人实际上并不需要流程来完成最好的工作。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And so, that, I think is always the tension that you have with process. And obviously one of the reasons why companies introduce process much more and more, as companies get bigger, is because it's harder to get all these folks who don't need processing. You actually want to reduce the variance.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为这始终是流程中的紧张因素。显然，随着公司规模的扩大，公司越来越多地引入流程的原因之一是因为很难找到所有不需要流程的人。您实际上想减少方差。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you're currently head of product at Retool, but before that you spent a lot of time at Stripe. You spent six years at Stripe. And so, before we get to Retool, I actually want to spend a little time on Stripe.
turns.zh: 您目前是 Retool 的产品主管，但在此之前您在 Stripe 工作了很多时间。您在 Stripe 工作了六年。因此，在我们开始 Retool 之前，我实际上想花一点时间在 Stripe 上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To set a little foundation, could you just talk about some of the things you worked on at Stripe? And maybe some of the things you're most proud of, during that time?
turns.zh: 为了打下基础，您能谈谈您在 Stripe 所做的一些事情吗？也许在那段时间里你最自豪的一些事情？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. So when I joined Stripe, I joined Stripe in 2013. It was pretty small at the time, it was around 50 people. And Stripe didn't have any product managers at that time.
turns.zh: 是的。所以当我加入Stripe时，我是在2013年加入Stripe的。当时规模很小，大约有50人。而且当时 Stripe 还没有产品经理。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think Stripe was kind of famous for that. And it really wasn't because we were anti-PM in any way. It was mostly just because we were building this product for developers. We had a lot of really talented engineers, who were essentially doing the PM job.
turns.zh: 我认为 Stripe 是因此而出名的。这确实不是因为我们在任何方面都反对总理。这主要是因为我们是为开发人员构建这个产品。我们有很多非常有才华的工程师，他们本质上是在做 PM 工作。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So I actually joined Stripe as the first account executive, which I think is pretty funny, now that I've seen real account executives do their jobs. Because I really just had no business doing that job. But it also really wasn't your typical sales job, in that most of Stripes volume was inbound. So I was really just spending all of my day talking to customers, helping them figure out how Stripe might work for their particular business flows, and payment models.
turns.zh: 所以我实际上作为第一位客户经理加入了 Stripe，我认为这很有趣，因为我已经看到了真正的客户经理在做他们的工作。因为我真的无权做那份工作。但这也确实不是典型的销售工作，因为大部分 Stripes 销量都是入境的。所以我实际上只是花了一整天的时间与客户交谈，帮助他们弄清楚 Stripe 如何适用于他们的特定业务流程和支付模式。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And a lot of it was, I think, what PMs do. It was just talking to customers, understanding their pain points, and really helping them figure out how the product might do that. And to this day, when people ask me, "Hey, what's your advice for going into product management?" I'm like, "Well, you should go get a sales job. I think it's pretty valuable."
turns.zh: 我认为，其中很多都是产品经理所做的。这只是与客户交谈，了解他们的痛点，并真正帮助他们弄清楚产品如何做到这一点。直到今天，当人们问我：“嘿，你对进入产品管理有什么建议？”我想，“好吧，你应该去找一份销售工作。我认为它很有价值。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But, it's kind of a long story to explain that, at the time there was this one sort of business model, the two-sided marketplace business model, that was just becoming huge. And you can't even really sort of imagine that now, but back then, Airbnb, Lyft, Uber, all those marketplaces, it was quite a new way of doing business.
turns.zh: 但是，要解释一下，当时有一种商业模式，即双边市场商业模式，它刚刚变得巨大，这是一个很长的故事。现在你甚至无法想象，但在当时，Airbnb、Lyft、Uber，所有这些市场，这是一种全新的经营方式。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And so, I was talking to all these customers and they had pretty complicated payment needs. So it was like, one payer putting in funds and it's getting paid out to a recipient. So an Airbnb guest and an Airbnb host. Or multiple payers putting funds in and it's getting paid out to one recipient, like a GoFundMe campaign. Or one payer putting in money and it going out to multiple recipients, like with ClassPass, where you get a subscription and then it gets paid out to a bunch of studios.
turns.zh: 因此，我与所有这些客户交谈，他们的付款需求非常复杂。就像，一个付款人投入资金，然后将资金支付给收款人。因此，一位 Airbnb 房客和一位 Airbnb 房东。或者多个付款人存入资金，然后将资金支付给一位收款人，就像 GoFundMe 活动一样。或者一个付款人投入资金，然后将资金发送给多个接收者，例如 ClassPass，您可以在其中获得订阅，然后将其支付给一群工作室。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then on top of that, all these platforms and marketplaces started having all these pretty complex regulatory and compliance requirements that were pretty different, country to country.
turns.zh: 最重要的是，所有这些平台和市场都开始有所有这些相当复杂的监管和合规要求，这些要求在不同国家之间有很大不同。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So it was just this really complicated financial infrastructure problem, and Stripe actually didn't really have the right solution for it. And no one else in the market did, either.
turns.zh: 所以这只是一个非常复杂的金融基础设施问题，而 Stripe 实际上并没有真正找到正确的解决方案。市场上也没有其他人这样做。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So at the time, this Stripe engineer, Brian Krausz, started poking around at this problem. Because I was talking to so many of these customers, we started talking about this problem together and poking around. And that actually resulted in us launching this sort of evolution of this product that we had at the time, called Stripe Connect.
turns.zh: 所以当时，Stripe 的工程师 Brian Krausz 开始研究这个问题。因为我和很多这样的客户交谈过，所以我们开始一起讨论这个问题并进行探索。这实际上导致我们推出了当时产品的这种演变，称为 Stripe Connect。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: That was easily, I think, one of my favorite products I worked on. Not only, it ended up actually being really quite significant for Stripe's business. But also, because it was the first product and I think that's always pretty special.
turns.zh: 我认为这很容易成为我最喜欢的产品之一。不仅如此，它实际上对 Stripe 的业务非常重要。而且，因为它是第一个产品，我认为它总是很特别。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, the second product that I think of very fondly during my time at Stripe, was this product, Stripe Radar. So Stripe obviously processes a lot of payments. Wherever there's money, fraudsters will kind of follow.
turns.zh: 然后，我在 Stripe 期间非常喜欢的第二个产品就是这个产品，Stripe Radar。所以 Stripe 显然处理了大量的付款。哪里有钱，哪里就有骗子跟风。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And there were certainly some merchants who were just particularly vulnerable to payments fraud. So, someone's using stolen credit card information to essentially purchase a good.
turns.zh: 当然，也有一些商家特别容易遭受支付欺诈。因此，有人使用被盗的信用卡信息来购买商品。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And if you're not in payments, this is going to sound kind of shocking. But if a merchant processes a payment from a customer and that customer used a stolen credit card, the merchant is ultimately on the hook for those funds. So it can be detrimental. The merchant who's trying to run a real business is just losing all of this money, because there are all of these frauds who are buying stuff from them online.
turns.zh: 如果你没有付款，这听起来有点令人震惊。但如果商家处理客户的付款，而该客户使用了被盗的信用卡，那么商家最终将承担这些资金的责任。所以这可能是有害的。试图经营真正业务的商人只会损失所有这些钱，因为所有这些欺诈者都在网上从他们那里购买东西。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So I really liked working on that product. So the product at Stripe was essentially, we built a bunch of machine learning models to try and predict when a payment was fraudulent. And then we built a product on top of that, to help customers understand why we were blocking payments, and help them write their own rules around that too.
turns.zh: 所以我真的很喜欢开发该产品。因此，Stripe 的产品本质上是，我们构建了一堆机器学习模型来尝试预测付款何时存在欺诈行为。然后我们在此基础上构建了一个产品，帮助客户了解我们阻止付款的原因，并帮助他们制定自己的规则。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And that was really fun, both from an anthropological perspective. Because we were kind of hanging out in corners of the internet where you wouldn't usually go if you were doing only legal things. So we were trying to understand who these fraudsters were.
turns.zh: 从人类学的角度来看，这真的很有趣。因为我们在互联网的某个角落闲逛，如果你只做合法的事情，你通常不会去那里。所以我们试图了解这些欺诈者是谁。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But it was also really cool from a product perspective, because of all the kind of complicated product questions around how humans should interact with AI and models. And I imagine a lot of the folks in the latest movement in AI are thinking a lot about that too. It's like, "How do you explain a model to humans? How do you let them interact with it?"
turns.zh: 但从产品的角度来看，它也非常酷，因为围绕人类应如何与人工智能和模型交互存在各种复杂的产品问题。我想人工智能最新运动中的很多人也正在思考这个问题。就像，“你如何向人类解释一个模型？你如何让他们与之互动？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So, both those things were really, really neat.
turns.zh: 所以，这两件事都非常非常整洁。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually use Stripe for my newsletter. It's how folks subscribe. And when I log into my Stripe Dashboard, there's so many products. I don't even know what many of them do. But I've often seen Radar being pitched to me as something I should pay for.
turns.zh: 实际上，我在时事通讯中使用了 Stripe。这就是人们订阅的方式。当我登录 Stripe 仪表板时，会看到很多产品。我什至不知道他们中的许多人是做什么的。但我经常看到雷达被推销给我，认为我应该付费。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I feel like I should probably turn it on. That sounds really useful.
turns.zh: 我觉得我应该打开它。听起来确实很有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One thing, that I want to dig in on... So you said when you joined, there were no PMs at Stripe. How many PMs were there when you moved into product at Stripe?
turns.zh: 我想深入探讨一件事......所以你说当你加入时，Stripe 没有产品经理。当您进入 Stripe 从事产品工作时，有多少位产品经理？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: That's a great question. I want to say maybe three or four.
turns.zh: 这是一个很好的问题。我想说也许三四个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Incredible.
turns.zh: 哇。极好的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you said Stripe is kind of known for being really late to PM and... I don't know if I want to say anti-PM, but there's a lot of sense of, "Why do we need PMs? We have amazing engineers who can decide what to build."
turns.zh: 你说 Stripe 因 PM 迟到而闻名……我不知道我是否想说反 PM，但有很多感觉，“为什么我们需要 PM？我们有出色的工程师，他们可以决定构建什么。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you can share around that general philosophy of Stripe? And was it effective? Was it good? Because a lot of companies are anti-PM. And I think they always point to Stripe, and Snap is another example of, "We don't need PMs. Look how far these companies got with without PMs."
turns.zh: 关于 Stripe 的总体理念，您有什么可以分享的吗？有效吗？好吗？因为很多公司都反对PM。我认为他们总是指向 Stripe，而 Snap 是另一个例子，“我们不需要 PM。看看这些公司在没有 PM 的情况下能走多远。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there something unique to Stripe that allowed them not to have PMs? I think there was like 200 employees probably, by the time they had their first PM.
turns.zh: Stripe 是否有什么独特之处使得他们不需要 PM？我认为，当他们有了第一位 PM 时，可能已经有 200 名员工了。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I think we actually had our first PM at... I want to say at about 100 employees.
turns.zh: 我认为我们的第一位 PM 实际上是在……我想说的是在大约 100 名员工中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But yeah, no, it was late in the game. And actually, maybe just to pattern match. Retool also didn't really have PMs for a while.
turns.zh: 但是，是的，不，比赛已经很晚了。实际上，也许只是为了模式匹配。 Retool 也有一段时间没有真正的产品经理了。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think actually both in the Stripe case and the Retool case, the thing that both of these companies have in common is, you're building for developers. The people who are building the product are the customers in a lot of ways. So, they get it. There's really no reason why you should have, in some ways, a middle man trying to figure out, "Hey, who's the customer, and what is it that they need?" And what are their pain points?"
turns.zh: 我认为实际上在 Stripe 案例和 Retool 案例中，这两家公司的共同点是，你都是为开发人员构建的。构建产品的人在很多方面都是客户。所以，他们明白了。在某些方面，你确实没有理由让一个中间人试图弄清楚，“嘿，谁是客户，他们需要什么？”他们的痛点是什么？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think the moment at which it became clear, "We really do need PMs at Stripe." And I think we felt the same way at Retool is, your customer base starts expanding. You start having different kinds of customers. You need to understand the whole market, all of the ICPs that you're going after.
turns.zh: 我认为在那个时刻，“我们确实需要 Stripe 的产品经理”这一点变得很清楚。我认为我们在 Retool 也有同样的感觉，您的客户群开始扩大。你开始拥有不同类型的客户。你需要了解整个市场，以及你所追求的所有 ICP。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And the organization gets more complex. I think Stripe... Gosh, in particular, it's just an extremely matrixed organization in business. Because every time you launch a product, you're having to think about, "Well, how do we do this in other countries? There's different financial infrastructure. How do we think about the legal side, the compliance side, et cetera?"
turns.zh: 而且组织变得更加复杂。我认为 Stripe...天哪，尤其是它只是一个极其矩阵化的商业组织。因为每次推出产品时，你都必须考虑，“那么，我们在其他国家如何做到这一点？那里有不同的金融基础设施。我们如何考虑法律方面、合规方面等等？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think PMs can really kind of bring that whole story together and make the whole machine move. In addition to understanding the customers, and the value prop, and what the overall strategy was.
turns.zh: 我认为产品经理确实可以将整个故事整合在一起并使整个机器运转起来。除了了解客户、价值支柱以及总体策略是什么之外。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good reminder of, engineers and designers can do the work of a PM, but often they don't want to. There's a lot of non-fun parts to it. They're like, "Oh, I wish we could have someone here do these things." And PMs enjoy that work. They're good at it. And so, eventually engineers and designers realize, "Okay, I see why maybe we should hire a PM."
turns.zh: 这确实很好地提醒了我们，工程师和设计师可以做产品经理的工作，但他们通常不愿意这样做。其中有很多不有趣的部分。他们就像，“哦，我希望我们能有人在这里做这些事情。”产品经理喜欢这项工作。他们很擅长。因此，最终工程师和设计师意识到，“好吧，我明白为什么我们应该聘请一名产品经理了。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I say this often actually, to folks who are thinking about going into product management. "That's awesome. Just be really, really sure about what you're signing up for."
turns.zh: 事实上，我经常对那些正在考虑进入产品管理的人说这句话。 “太棒了。只要非常非常确定您要注册的内容即可。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: It's kind of the same as, I think a lot of people want to become a manager. But just so you know, being a manager is like, "Hey, you're doing performance reviews a lot. And you're in one-on-ones a lot." You have to really love that kind of work. And I think in the product management case, it's also like, you're constantly working across a lot of different teams. You're trying to influence a lot of people who don't report into you directly, to do a bunch of stuff.
turns.zh: 这有点像，我认为很多人都想成为一名经理。但正如你所知，作为一名经理就像是，“嘿，你经常进行绩效评估。而且你经常进行一对一的谈话。”你必须真正热爱这种工作。我认为在产品管理案例中，你也经常在许多不同的团队中工作。你试图影响很多不直接向你汇报的人，去做很多事情。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And if you love that, that's great. But you've got to be sure you know you're signing up for it.
turns.zh: 如果你喜欢这个，那就太好了。但你必须确保你知道你正在注册。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's a really good comparison. When I first became a manager, I was an engineer, actually. And I was managing engineers. And then, when I moved on to something as an IC engineer, again, I was like, "I will never manage again. That was no fun at all. Why would I want to do this?"
turns.zh: 是的，这确实是一个很好的比较。当我第一次成为经理时，实际上我是一名工程师。我当时正在管理工程师。然后，当我再次担任 IC 工程师时，我想，“我再也不会管理了。那一点也不有趣。我为什么要这样做？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I imagine people get into product thinking they're going to have all this control, power, influence. And then they're like, "Oh my God, this job is so freaking crazy. What did I sign up for?"
turns.zh: 我想人们进入产品时会认为他们将拥有所有这些控制权、权力和影响力。然后他们会说，“天啊，这份工作太疯狂了。我报名干啥了？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: It's so hard.
turns.zh: 太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. That reminds me, something that I heard you did at Stripe is, you wrote their internal culture guide. It was like a quick start guide to culture at Stripe, that I think was maybe shared with early employees.
turns.zh: 是的。这让我想起，我听说你在 Stripe 所做的事情是，你写了他们的内部文化指南。这就像 Stripe 文化的快速入门指南，我认为可能会与早期员工分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And if that's true, I'm curious what it is about Stripe's culture? If you could just briefly share just what makes Stripe so special. Clearly, it's one of the most successful companies in the world, in history. I know there's been a a slowdown with the market. Everyone's slowed down a bit.
turns.zh: 如果这是真的，我很好奇 Stripe 的文化是什么？您能简单分享一下 Stripe 的特别之处吗？显然，它是历史上世界上最成功的公司之一。我知道市场正在放缓。大家都放慢了脚步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But it feels like Stripe has been incredibly successful and continues to innovate like crazy. Hires incredible people. People that are starting amazing companies.
turns.zh: 但感觉 Stripe 已经取得了令人难以置信的成功，并且继续疯狂创新。雇用了令人难以置信的人才。人们正在创办令人惊叹的公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I guess back to my question, what is it that you think makes Stripe's culture unique and special?
turns.zh: 所以我想回到我的问题，你认为是什么让 Stripe 的文化独一无二？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, that quick guide to Stripe's culture. I think we wrote it, maybe when we were around 150 people or so. And we actually wrote it to share with candidates.
turns.zh: 是的，这是 Stripe 文化的快速指南。我想我们大概是在 150 人左右的时候写的。我们写这篇文章实际上是为了与候选人分享。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Because the idea was like, "Look, we're kind of opinionated about how we do things here. Most companies struggle to describe what their culture is. Like, how does a fish describe water? But it's worthwhile getting a sense of the things that we feel opinionated about, and that you might like or you might not like."
turns.zh: 因为这个想法就像是，“看，我们对我们在这里做事的方式有点固执己见。大多数公司都很难描述他们的文化是什么。比如，鱼如何描述水？但值得了解我们认为固执己见的事情，以及你可能喜欢或可能不喜欢的事情。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And actually, when we put out the guide, our metric of success was that, more of the right people would apply to Stripe and fewer of the wrong people. And there was a whole section in there, I was like, "Hey, look, we work pretty hard here and that is certainly not for everyone. And hopefully you're excited to come and work really hard with colleagues who really care, and that's the reward." So, that's maybe one example.
turns.zh: 事实上，当我们发布指南时，我们衡量成功的标准是，更多合适的人会申请 Stripe，而更少的错误人会申请。那里有一个完整的部分，我想，“嘿，看，我们在这里工作非常努力，这当然不适合所有人。希望你很高兴能来和真正关心的同事一起努力工作，这就是奖励。”这也许就是一个例子。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: On Stripe's culture and what's made it so successful. I've really been thinking a lot about, "Were there one or two pivotal points or decisions for Stripe, that really set it on its path to success?" And I don't think there are, actually. Every time I'm like, "Well, if this hadn't happened..."
turns.zh: 关于 Stripe 的文化以及它如此成功的原因。我真的思考了很多，“对于 Stripe 来说，是否有一两个关键点或决定真正让它走上了成功之路？”事实上，我认为不存在。每次我都会想，“好吧，如果这件事没有发生的话……”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I can always reason my way into, "If these other things would've happened, Stripe would've kind of ended up in the same place."
turns.zh: 我总能推理出，“如果发生了这些其他事情，Stripe 也会陷入同样的​​境地。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So I think what Stripe was actually particularly good at... And by the way, you should take all this with a humongous grain of salt, because I haven't worked there since 2019. But, at least my experience when I was there, what Stripe was really good at was just making, not just one or two good decisions. It was making a lot of really good decisions all the time, big or small.
turns.zh: 所以我认为 Stripe 实际上特别擅长......顺便说一句，你应该对这一切持保留态度，因为我自 2019 年以来就没有在那里工作过。但是，至少根据我在那里的经验，Stripe 真正擅长的是做出，而不仅仅是一两个好的决定。它一直在做出很多非常好的决定，无论大小。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And that, I think, was quite cultural. There was this humongous respect and enthusiasm for thinking. It was such a part of the culture. One of the values was, think rigorously. Every meeting was very much like, "Hey, how do we think about this thing from first principle?"
turns.zh: 我认为这很有文化意义。人们对思考充满了极大的尊重和热情。这是文化的一部分。价值观之一是，严格思考。每次会议都非常像，“嘿，我们如何从第一原则考虑这件事？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: No one would ever say, for example, "It's a best practice to do X." People would be like, "Well, why?" You had to go a few levels deeper. So that was, I think, one piece.
turns.zh: 例如，没有人会说“做某件事是最佳实践”。人们会说，“嗯，为什么？”你必须更深入几个层次。所以我认为这是一件。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: The other piece... And a lot has been written about this already. Stripe had a very strong writing culture. All communication was along from writing business reviews, strategy memos, product reviews. There was a lot of writing that happened.
turns.zh: 另一件事情……关于这一点已经写了很多了。 Stripe 有着非常浓厚的写作文化。所有的沟通都是从撰写业务评论、战略备忘录、产品评论开始的。发生了很多写作。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I very strongly believe this. I don't think you can be a good writer, unless you're a clear thinker. And if you couldn't write well, I think it was actually pretty hard to be successful at Stripe, at least in the early days. So I think Stripe just cultivated a lot of really good writers, and by input into that, a lot of really good thinkers.
turns.zh: 我非常相信这一点。我不认为你能成为一名优秀的作家，除非你是一个清晰的思考者。如果你写得不好，我认为实际上很难在 Stripe 取得成功，至少在早期是这样。所以我认为 Stripe 培养了很多真正优秀的作家，并通过投入培养了很多真正优秀的思想家。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, I think the last thing that Stripe was really good at, was not overthinking decisions. Because that's kind of the flip side of this really rigorous approach, is that you lock yourself into a room and can't come out for five days. You have to be good at making a lot of decisions, and the right decisions, quickly.
turns.zh: 然后，我认为 Stripe 真正擅长的最后一件事就是不要过度思考决策。因为这是这种非常严格的方法的另一面，就是你把自己锁在一个房间里，五天内不能出来。你必须善于快速做出很多决定，而且是正确的决定。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And one of the things that we would always sort of kick around a lot was just the idea of, "Is it a trapdoor decision?" Which I think is an Amazon concept.
turns.zh: 我们经常讨论的一件事就是“这是一个活板门决定吗？”我认为这是亚马逊的概念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One-way door, or two-way door.
turns.zh: 单向门，或双向门。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: It's like, "If you make this decision, is it one door, or is it two doors? Can you come back from this decision?"
turns.zh: 就像，“如果你做出这个决定，是一扇门，还是两扇门？你能从这个决定中回来吗？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I thought Stripe was actually really good at being rigorous... Back to the rigorous point. About what actually was a trapdoor decision.
turns.zh: 我认为 Stripe 实际上非常擅长严谨……回到严谨的问题上来。关于什么实际上是一个活板门决定。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So I think a lot of people, for example, think pricing is a trapdoor decision. But actually, it's really easy to grandfather your existing users into some existing pricing model and change pricing for future users. And if you believe that the product's going to be successful, your early users are only going to be a fraction of that pricing model.
turns.zh: 例如，我认为很多人认为定价是一个暗门决策。但实际上，将现有用户纳入某些现有定价模型并更改未来用户的定价非常容易。如果您相信该产品将会成功，那么您的早期用户只是该定价模型的一小部分。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And if the product's not successful, then Who cares if you change the pricing model? So I think that's a really good example of, people think that's a trapdoor decision, but actually you can move much more quickly on that decision than you think.
turns.zh: 如果产品不成功，那么谁在乎你是否改变定价模式呢？所以我认为这是一个很好的例子，人们认为这是一个暗门决定，但实际上你可以比你想象的更快地做出这个决定。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, a decision that definitely felt to us very much like a trapdoor decision, that I think Stripe took a long time being really rigorous about, was titles. I think Stripe's kind of famous for not really having titles.
turns.zh: 然后，一个对我们来说绝对感觉非常像活板门决定的决定，我认为 Stripe 花了很长时间才非常严格，那就是标题。我认为 Stripe 因没有真正的头衔而出名。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think it was right to be rigorous around that decision, because once you've given someone a title, you can't really take it away. So you better be sure about the title you want to give someone.
turns.zh: 我认为严格执行这一决定是正确的，因为一旦你授予某人头衔，你就无法真正将其夺走。因此，您最好确定要授予某人的头衔。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, the titles are hilarious. I put together a career ladder doc of all company leveling names across all the big companies.
turns.zh: 是的，标题很搞笑。我整理了一份职业阶梯文档，其中包含所有大公司的所有公司级别名称。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Is everyone a lead, at Stripe?
turns.zh: Stripe 的每个人都是领导者吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's like, product manager, product manager, product manager, product manager... Yeah. And there's a lead here and there. Yeah, VPs are basically a product manager or a product leader, something like that.
turns.zh: 就像，产品经理，产品经理，产品经理，产品经理......是的。到处都有线索。是的，副总裁基本上是产品经理或产品领导者之类的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yep. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hilarious. You talked about this idea of first principles. People talk about that often as, "We want to be first principle thinkers. We're going to think from first principles."
turns.zh: 搞笑。您谈到了第一原则的想法。人们经常这样谈论这一点：“我们想成为第一原则思考者。我们将从第一原则出发思考。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How did Stripe actually operationalize that, implement that? Or was that just founder, top-down, continued questioning people, and that trickles down? Or is there anything else that they did to instill that mentality?
turns.zh: Stripe 是如何实际操作、实施的？或者只是创始人自上而下地不断向人们提问，然后慢慢渗透下去？或者他们还做了什么其他事情来灌输这种心态？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I definitely think it's founder, top-down. They were really good about hiring people who thought that way, too. So it's just all that stuff. It just really, really trickles.
turns.zh: 我绝对认为这是创始人，自上而下的。他们非常善于雇佣同样有这种想法的人。所以这就是所有这些东西。它真的非常非常细流。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And actually, to this day, when I'm preparing a memo, or a board deck, or something. I imagine in my head, I'm like, "What if I had to present this to Patrick?" And my ideas just get so much better, because I can sort of think about the questions they would ask.
turns.zh: 事实上，直到今天，当我准备一份备忘录、一份董事会报告或其他东西时。我在脑海中想象，“如果我必须把这个呈现给帕特里克怎么办？”我的想法变得更好，因为我可以思考他们会问的问题。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So, I think that was one. I think the other one was just sort of this writing culture piece. Once you start writing things down, you realize, "Hey, that actually doesn't make a lot of sense."
turns.zh: 所以，我认为这就是其中之一。我认为另一篇文章只是一种写作文化作品。一旦你开始写下来，你就会意识到，“嘿，这实际上没有多大意义。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, I think the third thing actually was, there was just always a lot of questioning about the status quo. So if something had been done in an industry for a long time, people would always be like, "Well, why was it done that way?"
turns.zh: 然后，我认为第三件事实际上是，人们总是对现状提出很多质疑。因此，如果某个行业已经做了很长时间的某件事，人们总是会问，“那么，为什么要这样做呢？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think this is actually how Stripe got its start. I think when Stripe started, if you wanted to set up a merchant account, it could take weeks. And everyone just assumed that's what it took. And of course John and Patrick were like, "Well, it doesn't actually make that much sense why it should take that long."
turns.zh: 我认为这实际上就是 Stripe 的起源。我认为，当 Stripe 开始时，如果你想建立一个商家帐户，可能需要几周的时间。每个人都认为这就是它所需要的。当然，约翰和帕特里克会说，“好吧，为什么要花那么长时间实际上没有多大意义。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You shared some of the values... I don't know if they're just called values, core values, at Stripe. But, is there other ones you can share? You said one is think rigorous, or don't overthink. What are the other values at Stripe?
turns.zh: 你分享了一些价值观......我不知道它们在 Stripe 是否只是被称为价值观、核心价值观。但是，还有其他可以分享的吗？你说一个人是想得严谨，还是别想太多。 Stripe 的其他价值观是什么？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, think rigorously was one. And I think they might have actually updated these on the website recently, so my recollection is very likely out of date.
turns.zh: 是的，严格思考就是其中之一。而且我认为他们可能最近在网站上更新了这些内容，所以我的记忆很可能已经过时了。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And Stripe would call them operating principles, actually. Which, I think is actually better. Because values, you can't really tell people what to value. Everyone has their own value set. But you can tell people like, "Hey, here's how we operate."
turns.zh: 事实上，Stripe 称它们为操作原则。我认为这实际上更好。因为价值观，你无法真正告诉人们该看重什么。每个人都有自己的价值观。但你可以告诉人们，“嘿，这就是我们的运作方式。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Another one that I loved was, move with urgency and focus. It was just really this idea that you're biggest compatriot and your biggest enemy as a startup, is time. So you have to move really, really, really fast on it.
turns.zh: 我喜欢的另一点是，紧迫而专注地行动。事实上，作为一家初创公司，时间是你最大的同胞，而你最大的敌人就是时间。所以你必须非常非常非常快地行动。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Customers first, was the other one. Or, users first, as Stripe would refer to customers as users. So those are some of my favorites.
turns.zh: 客户至上，是另一个。或者，用户第一，因为 Stripe 将客户称为用户。这些是我最喜欢的一些。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I think back to what made Airbnb special in a similar way, the values... We call them core values. I think were actually really, really important, and turned the company into what it ended up being. And I was actually there around the time they created these values.
turns.zh: 当我回想是什么让 Airbnb 以类似的方式如此特别时，价值观……我们称之为核心价值观。我认为它们实际上非常非常重要，并将公司变成了最终的样子。事实上，他们创造这些价值观的时候我就在场。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Oh, awesome.
turns.zh: 哦，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious, at Stripe, do you have any recollection of how they came to these operating principles? Because, as I mentioned, founders are listening. "How do I come up with these for our company?"
turns.zh: 我很好奇，在 Stripe，你还记得他们是如何得出这些运营原则的吗？因为，正如我提到的，创始人正在倾听。 “我如何为我们公司想出这些？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I'm pretty sure Patrick wrote them. Yeah. I think they came from... Patrick and John wrote them.
turns.zh: 我很确定帕特里克写了它们。是的。我认为它们来自……帕特里克和约翰写的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Actually, the other value that I love... I don't think they have it anymore, but it was good, the operating principles. Micro pessimists, macro optimists.
turns.zh: 事实上，我喜欢的另一个价值……我认为他们不再拥有它了，但它的运作原则很好。微观悲观主义者，宏观乐观主义者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. It was just this idea that, "In the long term, we expect the curve to go up. We very much believe in the upward trajectory of just about everything. But on the day-to-day decisions, on the minutiae, we're quite critical. How do we make sure this thing works?" And we'd think about all the ways in which it doesn't work.
turns.zh: 是的。正是这样的想法，“从长远来看，我们预计曲线会上升。我们非常相信几乎一切事物的上升轨迹。但在日常决策上，在细节上，我们非常挑剔。我们如何确保这件事发挥作用？”我们会思考它不起作用的所有方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So zooming out a little bit. We've been talking about Stripe. Retool also is a very first principles, innovative company.
turns.zh: 所以缩小一点。我们一直在谈论 Stripe。 Retool 也是一家秉持第一原则的创新型公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that I think of when I think of Retool is, during the wild market days of long ago, last year. I know Retool was very conservative in how they raised money, and the valuations they raised at. Which, looking back, ended up being a really good idea. While everyone's raising at $100 billion, I think their last round is a few billion. And it's a very reasonable, conservative way to think about fundraising.
turns.zh: 当我想到 Retool 时，我想到的是很久以前，也就是去年的疯狂市场时期。我知道 Retool 在融资方式以及融资估值方面非常保守。回想起来，这确实是一个好主意。虽然每个人都筹集了 1000 亿美元，但我认为他们的最后一轮融资是几十亿美元。这是一种非常合理、保守的筹款思考方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so, I guess just thinking about innovation in general. Why do you think some teams are able to run innovation machines, continue to put out new products, disrupt industries, while other companies kind of plod along and stay conservative?
turns.zh: 所以，我想只是考虑一般的创新。您认为为什么有些团队能够运行创新机器，不断推出新产品，颠覆行业，而其他公司却步履维艰并保持保守？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything you've seen, something you bring to teams you work on, to help foster innovation and big thinking?
turns.zh: 您是否见过任何东西，或者您给您工作的团队带来了什么，以帮助促进创新和大思维？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, I actually think about the extremes of that question. So not, "Why are some teams innovative?" But, "Why isn't every team innovative?" I feel like no one wakes up in the morning and thinks, "Yeah, today I want to work on boring, incremental stuff."
turns.zh: 是的，我实际上考虑过这个问题的极端情况。所以不是“为什么有些团队具有创新性？”但是，“为什么不是每个团队都具有创新精神？”我觉得没有人早上醒来会想：“是的，今天我想做一些无聊的、渐进的事情。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But, most teams do end up working on pretty incremental stuff. I always wonder, "What is it that's stopping folks from being creative and thinking bigger?" And I think it comes down to a couple of things that companies do sort of unwillingly, or not even realizing it.
turns.zh: 但是，大多数团队最终都会从事相当增量的工作。我总是想知道，“是什么阻碍了人们发挥创造力和思考更大的问题？”我认为这可以归结为公司不情愿地做了几件事，或者甚至没有意识到。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And one is this fear of failure. I think leaders want the upside of innovation, but they're not really willing to deal with the cost of innovation. Which is like, "Look, if you're going to swing big, you will invariably stumble sometimes."
turns.zh: 其中之一就是对失败的恐惧。我认为领导者希望获得创新的好处，但他们并不愿意承担创新的成本。这就像，“听着，如果你要挥杆很大，有时你总是会绊倒。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So I think if you want to mitigate that, you have to start shining light on failure. That's really the only way. You have to start normalizing it a little bit. And obviously, if an individual, or if a team is consistently failing and not learning. That, you need to deal with.
turns.zh: 所以我认为如果你想减轻这种情况，你必须开始关注失败。这确实是唯一的办法。你必须开始稍微规范化它。显然，如果一个人，或者一个团队不断失败并且不学习。那，你需要处理。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But I think sometimes it's good to fail. And when you do fail, use it as an opportunity. Don't squander that moment to not learn.
turns.zh: 但我认为有时候失败也是件好事。当你失败时，把它当作一个机会。不要浪费这一刻而不去学习。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But yeah, one example is, instead of calling something a postmortem, call it a retrospective, so that it's a positive thing. Like, "Hey, we're learning from this thing."
turns.zh: 但是，是的，一个例子是，不要将某件事称为事后剖析，而是将其称为回顾，所以这是一件积极的事情。就像，“嘿，我们正在从这件事中学习。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, I think the other way to kind of mitigate the feeling of failure is, you have to figure out how to give folks more at BATS. Because obviously, anything that takes one year to ship, and you haven't gotten any customer feedback, the stakes of that are just going to feel so, so high. If you get it wrong, it's going to be devastating. So you have to figure out how to lower the stakes.
turns.zh: 然后，我认为减轻失败感的另一种方法是，你必须弄清楚如何为 BATS 的人们提供更多。因为显然，任何需要一年时间才能发货的东西，而且你还没有得到任何客户反馈，那么这样做的风险就会感觉非常非常高。如果你弄错了，那将是毁灭性的。所以你必须弄清楚如何降低风险。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And honestly, I think in some ways it's kind of easy. It's like, "Look, don't put too many resources against these bigger swings. Have them be small teams." And then also, just get customer feedback as quickly as possible. Don't wait until the thing is perfect. And that way, you can limit the risk.
turns.zh: 老实说，我认为在某些方面这很容易。就像，“听着，不要投入太多资源来应对这些更大的波动。让他们成为小团队。”然后，尽快获得客户反馈。不要等到事情完美了才去做。这样，您就可以限制风险。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So yeah, I think fear of failure, that's definitely one thing that stops teams from being innovative.
turns.zh: 所以，是的，我认为对失败的恐惧，这绝对是阻止团队创新的一件事。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: There's a very practical one. Sometimes teams are just getting bogged down by really urgent work. There's too much tech debt. There's too much product debt. Bugs, instability. It's a massive hierarchy of needs. There's just no way that they're going to be able to focus on the enlightened, bigger, creative stuff if they're just heads-down dealing with incidents all day. So if that's the case, yeah, diagnose it and get your team out of that.
turns.zh: 有一个非常实用的。有时团队只是因为真正紧急的工作而陷入困境。科技债务太多了。产品债务太多了。错误，不稳定。这是一个巨大的需求层次。如果他们整天埋头处理事件，他们就不可能专注于开明的、更大的、有创造力的事情。所以如果是这种情况，是的，诊断一下并让你的团队摆脱困境。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, I think the last reason why teams aren't always that innovative is because, I think thinking big is really hard. And to some people it comes pretty naturally. But for most of us mortal souls, it's just really, really hard. And it takes time. And when you're at a startup and you're just grinding day-in, day-out, you're treading water just trying to make it through the day.
turns.zh: 然后，我认为团队不总是那么创新的最后一个原因是，我认为大胆思考真的很难。对于某些人来说，这是很自然的。但对于我们大多数凡人的灵魂来说，这真的非常非常困难。这需要时间。当你在一家初创公司时，你日复一日地苦苦挣扎，你就像在原地踏步，只是想度过这一天。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Taking the time to really think about the strategy, and where things should go, and get creative. It's pretty hard. So I call this... You have to give teams permission to think. So create these moments in your company culture, in your overall business processes, where you're asking people, you're literally saying, "Hey, this is part of your job to think bigger."
turns.zh: 花时间认真思考策略，以及事情应该走向何方，并发挥创造力。这很难。所以我称之为……你必须允许团队思考。因此，在你的公司文化、整个业务流程中创造这些时刻，当你询问人们时，你实际上是在说，“嘿，这是你工作的一部分，要思考更大的问题。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So at Retool, we have these team charters and we do team planning. And at the bottom of every team charter we have a section called, Think Bigger. "With 20% more time, what would you do that isn't on this list already?"
turns.zh: 因此，在 Retool，我们有这些团队章程并进行团队规划。在每个团队章程的底部，我们都有一个名为“思考更大”的部分。 “如果还有 20% 的时间，你会做哪些尚未在此清单上的事情？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then another really neat tradition that we had at Stripe, and we have a Retool now, too. Is this thing called, Crazy Ideas. So at the beginning of every year, David will send out a blank doc to the org and it's titled Crazy Ideas.
turns.zh: 然后，我们在 Stripe 拥有的另一个非常巧妙的传统，我们现在也有一个 Retool。这东西叫“疯狂的想法”吗？因此，每年年初，大卫都会向该组织发送一份空白文档，标题为“疯狂的想法”。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And the Prompt is, "Crazy ideas are ideas that we shouldn't, obviously, do. There's a 90% chance that they make no sense. But in the 10% chance that they do, they will make a 10x to 100x difference for the retail business." And then, it's literally just a request for crazy ideas.
turns.zh: 提示是，“显然，疯狂的想法是我们不应该做的想法。它们有 90% 的可能性毫无意义。但如果它们有 10% 的可能性，它们将为零售业务带来 10 倍到 100 倍的变化。”然后，这实际上只是对疯狂想法的请求。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And the org loves it. It's amazing. The energy around it is so cool. And it's not just product ideas, it's different ways of how we should run our organization. Or, it's really cool marketing ideas in there.
turns.zh: 该组织喜欢它。太棒了。周围的能量是如此的凉爽。这不仅仅是产品创意，更是我们运营组织的不同方式。或者，这里面的营销理念真的很酷。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So, that doc is awesome. And whenever I have a down day, I just scroll through that doc.
turns.zh: 所以，那个医生很棒。每当我心情低落时，我就会滚动浏览该文档。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that you've launched three different products this year which I want to talk about, which maybe came out of this big thinking. But a couple more questions just to dig into some of the stuff you just shared.
turns.zh: 我知道你们今年推出了三种不同的产品，我想谈谈这三种产品，这可能是出于这个大的思考。但还有几个问题只是为了深入了解您刚刚分享的一些内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One is this big doc of awesome ideas. What's come out of that? Because I think of hackathons, and people have all this energy, and it's exciting. And then they do all these cool things and they don't go anywhere.
turns.zh: 其中之一就是这个包含了很棒想法的大文档。结果是什么呢？因为我想到了黑客马拉松，人们充满活力，这令人兴奋。然后他们做了所有这些很酷的事情，但他们哪儿也不去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do things come out of this? Does it lead to actual ideas that people follow up on?
turns.zh: 事情是这样产生的吗？它是否会带来人们跟进的实际想法？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. So every year that we send out the doc, we look at the doc from the past year, and we're like, "Okay, did we do anything on this list?" And consistently, we do anywhere between three to eight things on the list.
turns.zh: 是的。是啊是啊。因此，每年我们发出文档时，我们都会查看过去一年的文档，然后我们会想，“好吧，我们在这个清单上做了什么吗？”我们始终如一地做清单上的三到八件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of a product that launched, that came from that list, that comes to mind?
turns.zh: 是否有一个来自该列表的已推出产品的示例？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Actually, at least one, if not two of the three products that we launched this last year were on the crazy ideas list at one point. Like, a year ago, if you'd asked me, "What is Retool's product?" I would've told you, "Retool helps you build internal frontends really, really fast."
turns.zh: 事实上，我们去年推出的三种产品中，至少有一种（如果不是两种）曾一度出现在疯狂创意清单上。就像一年前，如果你问我“Retool 的产品是什么？”我会告诉你，“Retool 可以帮助你非常非常快地构建内部前端。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But if you were trying to schedule a query to run at a later point in time, or have something trigger, or run an ETL task, you couldn't do that in Retool. So that was actually one of the crazy ideas. And that ended up becoming Retool Workflows, which we launched just last year, in November.
turns.zh: 但是，如果您尝试安排查询在稍后的时间点运行，或者有某些触发器，或者运行 ETL 任务，则无法在 Retool 中执行此操作。所以这实际上是疯狂的想法之一。这最终成为我们去年 11 月刚刚推出的 Retool Workflows。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. We're definitely going to chat a bit about that. I want to go back to the two other suggestions you had. One is embrace failure, make it okay to fail. And then two is, don't let people get sucked into urgent stuff, and have time to focus on important stuff.
turns.zh: 好的。我们肯定会讨论一下这个问题。我想回到你提出的另外两个建议。一是拥抱失败，接受失败。第二点是，不要让人们陷入紧急的事情中，而有时间专注于重要的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of just how to help people embrace failure? You talked about retrospectives. Is there anything else that you've found works, either as a tactic, as a process, as a framework, just to help people get out of that?
turns.zh: 有没有一个例子可以说明如何帮助人们接受失败？你谈到了回顾。您是否发现还有其他有效的方法，无论是作为策略、过程还是框架，只是为了帮助人们摆脱困境？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because I hear that a lot, "Embrace failure." And then people are like, "Oh, but I failed and I suck." So yeah, is there anything else along those lines that you found effective to create that feeling?
turns.zh: 因为我经常听到“拥抱失败”。然后人们会说，“哦，但我失败了，我很糟糕。”那么，是的，您认为还有其他什么可以有效地创造这种感觉吗？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: To me, it's always in the follow-ups. So have people talk about the failure in these sort of public forums, where usually you talk about the successes. So have someone actually write a note that's like, "Hey, here are all my learnings from this thing that we did." And send it to the org.
turns.zh: 对我来说，它总是在后续行动中。因此，人们在这类公共论坛上谈论失败，而通常你在这些论坛上谈论成功。因此，请有人实际写一张便条，例如“嘿，这是我从我们所做的这件事中学到的所有教训。”并将其发送给组织。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: At Retool we have a shipped email list. If you ship something, you'll always send to that.
turns.zh: 在 Retool，我们有一份已发货的电子邮件列表。如果你运送东西，你总是会发送到那里。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Have them send that email to the org. It's just an awesome way to celebrate. Or have them present it all-hands and share what they learned. And it almost always results in, I think, a really positive twist.
turns.zh: 让他们将该电子邮件发送给组织。这只是一种很棒的庆祝方式。或者让他们全体展示并分享他们学到的东西。我认为，它几乎总是会带来真正积极的转变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: At Airbnb, I think for a period, there was an award for the biggest failure project and feature.
turns.zh: 我认为在 Airbnb，有一段时间，最大的失败项目和功能被授予了一个奖项。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Really? That's so cool.
turns.zh: 真的吗？太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, like a trophy or something. It was a short-lived idea, but it was funny.
turns.zh: 是的，比如奖杯什么的。这是一个短暂的想法，但很有趣。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊，是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then, on the second bullet point of urgency, giving people a chance to think longer term. Is there anything there, that you found to be actually effective, to create that culture, and give PMs and product teams a chance to think longer term, and not just be stuck in the fires that they're dealing with?
turns.zh: 然后，在第二个紧迫问题上，让人们有机会进行更长远的思考。您发现有什么实际上有效的方法可以创建这种文化，并让产品经理和产品团队有机会进行更长远的思考，而不仅仅是陷入困境？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: There's a couple of top-down things, and a couple of bottom-up things.
turns.zh: 有一些自上而下的事情，还有一些自下而上的事情。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: On the top-down, sometimes you just have to be willing to fund someone with something. Like, they come to you with an idea and you're like, "Look, yeah, take an engineer and go do it." And you just have to give folks that sort of organizational buy-in.
turns.zh: 从上到下，有时你只需要愿意用某些东西资助某人即可。就像，他们带着一个想法来找你，你会说，“看，是的，带一个工程师去做吧。”你只需要给予人们这种组织上的支持。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Actually, I was thinking back to that engineer, Brian Krausz at Stripe, who started poking around on this marketplace model. And I was thinking, I can't remember a moment when someone formally said to him, "This is now your job." I think he just went and looked, and went and dug into it. And at some point, I think a manager was like, "All right, this is now your job."
turns.zh: 事实上，我回想起了 Stripe 的工程师 Brian Krausz，他开始研究这个市场模型。我在想，我不记得何时有人正式对他说：“现在这是你的工作了。”我认为他只是去看了看，然后去深入研究。在某些时候，我认为经理会说，“好吧，现在这是你的工作了。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But yeah, no, I think you have to be able to fund folks' time and give that. Hackathons, I think, are pretty good for that stuff. It is kind of a moment for folks to take a step back.
turns.zh: 但是，是的，不，我认为你必须能够资助人们的时间并给予他们。我认为，黑客马拉松非常适合这些东西。现在是人们退后一步的时刻。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, I think more than anything, in people's planning processes, I really like asking folks the 20% more time question. Or the other question was, "Look, if you doubled the team today, what would you do?" That shows up in our planning processes as well.
turns.zh: 然后，我认为最重要的是，在人们的计划过程中，我真的很喜欢问人们“多花 20% 时间”的问题。或者另一个问题是，“看，如果你今天将球队加倍，你会做什么？”这也体现在我们的规划流程中。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think it really helps people kind of break out of this... I think you end up planning towards the team that you have and not the team that you should have. So, that's how folks can break out of that process.
turns.zh: 我认为这确实可以帮助人们摆脱困境......我认为你最终会为你拥有的团队而不是你应该拥有的团队进行规划。所以，这就是人们如何摆脱这个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I really like the think bigger bucket in your planning docs. Just like, "What would you do if you had more resources?" Maybe a quick question there. Is there a bunch of detail that you ask them to put into that, or is it just a bullet point of big ideas?
turns.zh: 惊人的。我真的很喜欢你的规划文档中的“思考更大的桶”。就像“如果你有更多资源你会做什么？”也许有一个简单的问题。您是否要求他们提供大量细节，或者只是一些重要想法的要点？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Folks can just go crazy on it. It's however they want to take it. I've seen folks actually create entire demos.
turns.zh: 人们可能会为之疯狂。然而他们想接受它。我见过人们实际上创建了整个演示。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But I actually think the trick is less structure, in those cases. Because you don't really want to sort of pigeonhole... Or make it even that intimidating for folks. If someone just wants to write down a few bullets, that's great.
turns.zh: 但我实际上认为在这些情况下，诀窍在于减少结构。因为你真的不想把事情归为一类……或者让人们感到害怕。如果有人只想写下一些要点，那就太好了。

turns.zh: 本集由 Eppo 为您带来。 Eppo 是下一代 A/B 测试平台，由 Airbnb 校友为现代增长团队打造。 Netlify、Contentful 和 Cameo 等公司依靠 Eppo 来支持他们的实验。

turns.zh: 无论您在哪里工作，进行实验都变得越来越重要，但是没有可以与现代增长团队堆栈集成的商业工具。这会导致浪费时间构建内部工具，或尝试通过笨重的营销工具进行实验。
