turns.zh: 请访问 GetEppo.com 查看 Eppo。获取 E-P-P-O.com，让您的实验速度提高 10 倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so you launched three new products this year. Usually, companies are lucky to launch one product a year. A few questions.
turns.zh: 好的，今年你们推出了三款新产品。通常，公司很幸运能够每年推出一款产品。有几个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One, just tell us what those three were, in case people are interested and want to check them out. Two is, was that a good idea? Is it good to launch three new products in a year?
turns.zh: 第一，请告诉我们这三个是什么，以防人们感兴趣并想查看它们。二是，这是个好主意吗？一年推出三款新品好吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then three, what did you do organizationally, to allow for this to happen? Because that feels really ambitious and rare, and I'm curious what you learned from that.
turns.zh: 第三，为了让这种情况发生，你在组织上做了什么？因为这感觉非常雄心勃勃且罕见，我很好奇你从中学到了什么。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So the three products we launched, one was Retool Workflows that I talked to you a little bit about. It's like, if you want to be able to, essentially create a workflow. Like schedule an alert, run a task, you can kind of do it in the Retool way. Where it's this visual, sort of easier builder of creating these different sort of workflows. But you can write your own code on top of it, as well.
turns.zh: 因此，我们推出了三个产品，其中一个是我与您讨论过的“重组工作流程”。就像，如果您希望能够创建一个工作流程。就像安排警报、运行任务一样，您可以通过 Retool 方式来完成。正是这种视觉效果，让创建这些不同类型的工作流程变得更加容易。但您也可以在其上编写自己的代码。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: The second product is Retool Mobile. So you could pretty easily build incredible web apps with Retool. But there are plenty of folks who don't sit behind their laptop at a desk all day. And for those folks... We had a lot of companies who were like, "I want a mobile native app." And so, we launched that product.
turns.zh: 第二个产品是Retool Mobile。因此，您可以使用 Retool 轻松构建令人难以置信的 Web 应用程序。但有很多人不会整天坐在办公桌前的笔记本电脑后面。对于那些人来说......我们有很多公司都说，“我想要一个移动原生应用程序。”因此，我们推出了该产品。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then the third product was Retool Database. So until very recently, if you came to Retool, you could connect your data via your APIs, your database, directly into Retool.
turns.zh: 然后第三个产品是Retool Database。因此，直到最近，如果您使用 Retool，您可以通过 API、数据库将数据直接连接到 Retool。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But what we found is that actually, a lot of folks either don't have access to their database, or they're just trying to build an internal tool and they don't necessarily want to store that data in their production database.
turns.zh: 但我们发现，实际上，很多人要么无法访问他们的数据库，要么他们只是试图构建一个内部工具，并且他们不一定希望将该数据存储在他们的生产数据库中。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So we built... Essentially, we spin up a post [inaudible 00:33:32] database for you. And you can just access it via a really nice UI and manage it directly in Retool.
turns.zh: 所以我们建立了......本质上，我们为您建立了一个帖子 [听不清 00:33:32] 数据库。您可以通过一个非常漂亮的 UI 访问它并直接在 Retool 中管理它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, back to the other two questions.
turns.zh: 惊人的。好吧，回到另外两个问题。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yes. Okay. So I think your second question was, "Was this a good idea?"
turns.zh: 是的。好的。所以我认为你的第二个问题是，“这是个好主意吗？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 正确的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. You know what? I think in hindsight, if I were to do it again, I think sequencing it would've been slightly better. Just because, I think what we ended up doing is, we ended up launching the idea behind all three of these products at around the same time. And they all ended up maturing at around the same time, and that was just a lot of headspace from the org. Even though actually, the teams themselves were not that big.
turns.zh: 是的。你知道吗？事后看来，如果我再做一次，我认为排序会更好一些。只是因为，我认为我们最终所做的是，我们最终大约在同一时间推出了所有这三个产品背后的想法。他们几乎在同一时间成熟，这只是组织的大量顶空。尽管实际上，团队本身并没有那么大。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: It was just like, we had all these products and we were just waiting for them to launch and waiting for them to launch. Whereas, maybe if we'd sequenced it, I think that would've felt more satisfying to the whole organization.
turns.zh: 就像我们拥有所有这些产品，我们只是在等待它们推出并等待它们推出。然而，也许如果我们对其进行排序，我认为整个组织都会感到更满意。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But, I mean, it ended up working out. I think that's kind of the crazy thing. It's like, we were able to pull off launching these three products.
turns.zh: 但是，我的意思是，它最终成功了。我认为这有点疯狂。就像我们能够成功推出这三款产品一样。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And by the way, I should caveat that, the further I get along my career, the more I realize I'm just kind of building on the shoulders of giants. And a lot of these ideas, et cetera, were very much in the works and were happening before I came along.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我应该警告一下，我的职业生涯越深入，我就越意识到我只是站在巨人的肩膀上。很多这样的想法等等，在我出现之前就已经在酝酿之中并且已经发生了。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But yeah, it was really neat to see how we got that all over the finish line in a year.
turns.zh: 但是，是的，看到我们如何在一年内冲过终点线真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then, the last question there is just, what do you think you did to allow for this? Because it's pretty rare you can build so much. And I know the team's not huge. How many people work at Retool, roughly?
turns.zh: 然后，最后一个问题是，你认为你做了什么来允许这种情况发生？因为你能建造这么多东西是非常罕见的。我知道这个团队并不庞大。 Retool 大约有多少人？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Today, we're around 300 people.
turns.zh: 今天，我们大约有 300 人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So how do you structure an org to build three and launch... I didn't realize they launched around the same time. It's like, I'm picturing Elon Musk launching three rockets at once. How do you allow for that to happen?
turns.zh: 是的。那么，如何构建一个组织来构建三个并启动......我没有意识到他们大约在同一时间启动。就像，我想象埃隆·马斯克同时发射三枚火箭。你如何允许这种情况发生？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, I'm sure our product marketing team felt that way. Yeah, a couple of things. We started really small with all of these initiatives.
turns.zh: 是的，我确信我们的产品营销团队也有这种感觉。是的，有几件事。我们从所有这些举措开始都是很小的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So I think I mentioned, we really had one or two people working on each of these products for the first six months. So it was one engineer and one designer, or one engineer and one PM. And they really didn't get funding until it was clear that there was something there.
turns.zh: 所以我想我提到过，在前六个月里，我们确实有一两个人在开发这些产品。所以是一名工程师和一名设计师，或者一名工程师和一名产品经理。直到人们清楚地知道那里有什么东西，他们才真正获得资金。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So those teams, they spent a ton of time with customers. They spent a ton of time building, a ton of time prototyping. And it was kind of the moment where it was like, "Okay, they are there." That we started bringing more people onto the team.
turns.zh: 所以这些团队花了很多时间与客户打交道。他们花费了大量时间进行构建、原型设计。那一刻就像是，“好吧，他们就在那里。”我们开始让更多的人加入团队。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So, that was the first piece. The second piece is that, we really treated them like startups. We're like, Retool's the VC, and Retool funds with resources and Retool's existing customer base. Which is obviously quite valuable, because you have all these customers you can market to and promote to.
turns.zh: 所以，这是第一件作品。第二点是，我们真的像对待初创公司一样对待他们。我们就像，Retool 是风险投资家，Retool 拥有资源和 Retool 现有客户群的资金。这显然是非常有价值的，因为你拥有所有可以向其进行营销和推广的客户。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But then, the teams really had to prove that ROI. Either in engagement, or eventually revenue, in order to be able to move forward.
turns.zh: 但随后，团队确实必须证明投资回报率。无论是参与度，还是最终的收入，以便能够向前发展。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then the third thing... And this one, actually I think it can be quite controversial. Is, we were really deliberate about keeping these teams separate from the rest of the org, especially early on. Now, a lot of them, they're very much a part of the overall organizational processes.
turns.zh: 然后第三件事......实际上，我认为这可能是很有争议的。是的，我们确实有意将这些团队与组织的其他部分分开，尤其是在早期。现在，他们中的很多人已经成为整个组织流程的一部分。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But very early on, they were running on their own. They were meeting quite independently with one, or two, or three folks from the leadership team. And they were also just quite separate from the product itself.
turns.zh: 但很早的时候，他们就在自己运行。他们非常独立地与领导团队中的一两个或三个人会面。而且它们也与产品本身完全分开。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I think Retool Mobile's actually a really good example, where we had a lot of debate about whether or not we should build Retool Mobile out of the core web app builder. Because a lot of the primitives are the same.
turns.zh: 我认为 Retool Mobile 实际上是一个很好的例子，我们就是否应该从核心 Web 应用程序构建器中构建 Retool Mobile 进行了很多争论。因为很多原语都是相同的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And we eventually decided that we were going to run it as a separate team, because we wanted the team to be able to move really, really quickly. And we didn't want it to get bogged down in, what are just the realities of running a product that has product market fit, like bugs, yada, yada, et cetera.
turns.zh: 我们最终决定将其作为一个单独的团队来运营，因为我们希望团队能够非常非常快地行动。我们不希望它陷入困境，运行一个适合产品市场的产品的现实是什么，比如 bug、yada、yada 等等。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think that was absolutely the right call, because Retool Mobile actually has quite a different target customer. Which, we only really realized maybe like halfway through the project. And I don't think we would've been able to really understand that, or even get broader in that kind of thinking, had we sort of been stuck in the core retail product.
turns.zh: 我认为这绝对是正确的选择，因为 Retool Mobile 实际上有一个完全不同的目标客户。我们直到项目进行到一半才真正意识到这一点。我认为，如果我们一直停留在核心零售产品上，我们就无法真正理解这一点，甚至无法扩大这种思维。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But yeah, there was a cost to that, too. Which is like, "Okay, now we have these two products, and we have to..." I think obviously the strength will be, "How do all these products interact with each other, and how do they build on top of each other?"
turns.zh: 但是，是的，这也是有代价的。就像，“好吧，现在我们有了这两种产品，我们必须......”我认为显然优势将是，“所有这些产品如何相互作用，以及它们如何相互构建？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So, we have to go and invest in that now. But I think it's totally worth it, because your team can just move more quickly, be more independent, and think more independently, too.
turns.zh: 所以，我们现在必须去投资。但我认为这是完全值得的，因为你的团队可以更快地行动，更加独立，也更加独立思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the time that you worked at Stripe and Retool... I know we chatted before we started recording. You think a lot about, "What is the right level of process for companies at different stages?"
turns.zh: 当你在 Stripe 和 Retool 工作的时候……我知道我们在开始录音之前聊过。你经常思考“对于处于不同阶段的公司来说，合适的流程水平是什么？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I'd love to just hear your thoughts, because I know that's a challenge a lot of companies face. "How much do we put in now? Do we get inspiration from big companies? Do we try to stay lean?"
turns.zh: 我很想听听您的想法，因为我知道这是很多公司面临的挑战。 “我们现在投入了多少？我们是否从大公司获得灵感？我们是否努力保持精益？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something here, that we actually run into. I'll just mention briefly that, there was a huge resistance to process for a long time. And so the product team was just kind of a little crazy for a bit. And then we were like, "Okay, we need product development process. We need deadlines and specs." And that helped a lot.
turns.zh: 我们实际上遇到了一些东西。我只想简单提一下，长期以来，流程面临着巨大的阻力。所以产品团队有一段时间有点疯狂。然后我们说，“好吧，我们需要产品开发流程。我们需要截止日期和规格。”这很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let me ask again, just how do you think about the right level of process for a stage of company, and what have you learned there?
turns.zh: 那么我再问一遍，您如何看待公司某个阶段的正确流程水平？您从中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. What I would really love from companies is just sort of like this time capsule, where you can see what their processes were when they were like 20 people, and 50 people, and 100 people, and 500 people.
turns.zh: 是的。我真正喜欢的公司就是这样一个时间胶囊，你可以在其中看到他们有 20 人、50 人、100 人、500 人时的流程。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Because when we were at Stripe and we were trying to figure out our planning process, we actually talked to Amazon, and Atlassian, and Apple, and all these companies that we really, really respect and look up to.
turns.zh: 因为当我们在 Stripe 时，我们试图弄清楚我们的规划流程，我们实际上与亚马逊、Atlassian、苹果以及所有这些我们非常非常尊重和仰慕的公司进行了交谈。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I remember taking down notes from these companies and being like, "Yeah, this is awesome, but there's no way that this will work for Stripe." Stripe was so much smaller than any of these companies.
turns.zh: 我记得我记下了这些公司的笔记，然后说：“是的，这太棒了，但这对 Stripe 来说是行不通的。” Stripe 比这些公司都小得多。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So yeah, they were showing us where we had to go, but no idea how to get there. And so, yeah, Lenny, maybe you can help us figure out time capsules for companies and what processes make sense.
turns.zh: 是的，他们向我们展示了我们必须去的地方，但不知道如何到达那里。所以，是的，莱尼，也许你可以帮助我们找出公司的时间胶囊以及哪些流程有意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I am working on that, roughly.
turns.zh: 是的。我正在做这方面的工作，大概是这样。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Oh, nice.
turns.zh: 哦，不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going company by company, about how they think process and about process. And then maybe I'll check in every couple of years.
turns.zh: 我逐家询问他们如何看待流程以及流程。然后也许我会每隔几年检查一次。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Cool. I love that. But yeah, to answer your question directly. Process... Yeah, it really gives people a bitter taste in their mouth, I think.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。我喜欢那个。但是，是的，直接回答你的问题。过程……是的，我觉得确实让人嘴里有苦涩的味道。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Process, by definition, is variance reducing. You're introducing it, because you worry that the variance in your org is too high. You want people to sort of meet a certain standard.
turns.zh: 根据定义，过程是减少方差的过程。您之所以引入它，是因为您担心组织中的差异太大。你希望人们达到一定的标准。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And the cost of that is obviously, while you are reducing the standard and bringing folks up to the average, you're also bringing other folks down to the average. And oftentimes, the folks you're bringing down are your highest performers, your most creative thinkers. The folks who, I think actually don't really need process to do their best work.
turns.zh: 这样做的代价显然是，当你降低标准并使人们达到平均水平时，你也将其他人降低到平均水平。通常，你打倒的人是你表现最好的人、你最有创造力的思想家。我认为这些人实际上并不需要流程来完成最好的工作。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And so, that, I think is always the tension that you have with process. And obviously one of the reasons why companies introduce process much more and more, as companies get bigger, is because it's harder to get all these folks who don't need processing. You actually want to reduce the variance.
turns.zh: 因此，我认为这始终是流程中的紧张因素。显然，随着公司规模的扩大，公司越来越多地引入流程的原因之一是因为很难找到所有不需要流程的人。您实际上想减少方差。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: This is actually a little bit of an aside, but it's kind of relevant, so I'm just going to mention it. And you can feel free to let me know if it's too much of an aside.
turns.zh: 这实际上有点题外话，但它有点相关，所以我只想提一下。如果这是多余的，你可以随时告诉我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's get into it.
turns.zh: 让我们开始吧。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But, I was just listening to this awesome podcast with Russ Roberts, who's a professor. He hosts EconTalk. I don't know if you listen to it.
turns.zh: 但是，我只是在听拉斯·罗伯茨（Russ Roberts）教授的精彩播客。他主持 EconTalk。我不知道你是否听过。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And he was in interviewing this guy, Ian Leslie, who's this great writer and has just written this article that's... Basically, something along the lines of what it means to be human in the age of AI.
turns.zh: 他正在采访这个人，伊恩·莱斯利（Ian Leslie），他是一位伟大的作家，刚刚写了这篇文章……基本上，与人工智能时代人类的意义相似。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I thought he just articulated this idea well. Which is, we're all really so impressed when we see ChatGPT-3 spit out this piece of writing that feels very human-like.
turns.zh: 我认为他很好地表达了这个想法。也就是说，当我们看到 ChatGPT-3 吐出这篇感觉非常人性化的文章时，我们都非常印象深刻。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But what we're kind of forgetting is that, over the last 10, 20, 30 years, we're actually asking humans to be a lot more robot-like. In that, we're really asking everyone to standardize in a lot of ways. And we're making people a lot more formulaic. If you think about how we teach people to write, it's like, "Well, there's five paragraphs. And there's your opening paragraph. And you state your topic."
turns.zh: 但我们有点忘记的是，在过去的 10 年、20 年、30 年里，我们实际上要求人类变得更像机器人。在这方面，我们确实要求每个人在很多方面都实现标准化。我们正在让人们变得更加公式化。如果你想想我们如何教人们写作，就像是，“嗯，有五个段落。这是你的开头段落。然后你陈述你的主题。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So anyway, I think the point is, the more formulaic, the more sort of mass produced you're trying to make something. The more you kind of quench people's creativity, and the further away you get from the really, really high highs. And that, to me, is the cost of process, and rules, and templates.
turns.zh: 所以无论如何，我认为重点是，你想要制作的东西越公式化，就越能大规模生产。你越是抑制人们的创造力，你离真正的巅峰就越远。对我来说，这就是流程、规则和模板的成本。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So if you're going to introduce it, be really, really sure that you're okay with that cost. And give folks escape hatches.
turns.zh: 因此，如果您打算推出它，请务必非常确定您可以接受该成本。并为人们提供逃生舱口。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So I've started referring to this as the MVP, the minimum viable process. So if I give folks a template, I'm like, "Look, use the template. But if you want to break out of it, please absolutely do." And I've started writing this at the top of templates now.
turns.zh: 所以我开始将其称为 MVP，即最小可行流程。因此，如果我给人们一个模板，我会说，“看，使用该模板。但如果你想打破它，请绝对这样做。”我现在已经开始在模板顶部编写此内容。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: It's like, "If this doesn't work for what you're trying to explain, don't use it. But just know that this is the minimum viable thing. We're setting the bar here, but go higher if you can, please."
turns.zh: 就像是，“如果这对你想要解释的内容不起作用，就不要使用它。但要知道这是最低限度可行的事情。我们在这里设定了标准，但如果可以的话，请提高一点。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So anyway, that's my sort of long drive on process. With all that said, I do think that companies, there's just a set of documents that are really, really viable. That every sort of level of the organization should have throughout its lifecycle.
turns.zh: 不管怎样，这就是我的一个漫长的过程。话虽如此，我确实认为公司只有一套真正可行的文件。组织的各个级别都应该在其整个生命周期中拥有这一点。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, I think how sort of involved it is, or how long term it is really depends on how big you are.
turns.zh: 然后，我认为它的参与程度，或者它的持续时间有多长，实际上取决于你的规模有多大。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But those documents, to me, are the charter. So, "What is your mission, your vision and your strategy?" The goals, "What are you aiming to do and how are you going to measure success?" And then the roadmap, "What is the thing that you're shipping?"
turns.zh: 但对我来说，这些文件就是章程。那么，“你的使命、愿景和战略是什么？”目标是“你的目标是什么？你将如何衡量成功？”然后是路线图，“您要运送的东西是什么？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think the whole company needs these, the whole function. So in product, you need all three of these. And then, within each team you need all three of these.
turns.zh: 我认为整个公司都需要这些，整个职能。所以在产品中，你需要这三个。然后，在每个团队中，您都需要这三者。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I've kind of noticed two things about this framework for myself. One, I've actually noticed that teams often work their way from the bottom-up, versus top-down. They start with a roadmap. They're like, "What are all the things we're going to ship?" Especially early on. And then they kind of work their way into a charter. But I think it's really, really worth it to start from the top-down.
turns.zh: 我自己注意到了关于这个框架的两件事。第一，我实际上注意到团队通常是自下而上而不是自上而下地工作。他们从路线图开始。他们会问，“我们要运送什么东西？”尤其是早期。然后他们就制定了章程。但我认为从自上而下开始确实非常值得。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, the second thing that I've noticed is that your time horizon really shifts as you get more mature. So if you're very early on, you don't have PMF, you should have a charter, but your charter should be like three months in the future. Because you can't look that much further.
turns.zh: 然后，我注意到的第二件事是，随着你变得更加成熟，你的时间范围确实会发生变化。因此，如果您很早，没有 PMF，您应该有一份章程，但您的章程应该是未来三个月的时间。因为你不能看得那么远。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And if you're a company that's humming and going, your charter is probably... The horizon's maybe a decade.
turns.zh: 如果您是一家蓬勃发展的公司，那么您的章程可能是……期限可能是十年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. There is so much there. I could go into so many different directions. One thing I wanted to follow up on a little bit, is this idea... Such a great point. That process brings the best people down and kind of averages them out to create consistency.
turns.zh: 哇。那里有很多东西。我可以进入很多不同的方向。我想跟进的一件事是这个想法......真是一个伟大的观点。这个过程会降低最优秀的人才的水平，并对他们进行平均，以保持一致性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I'm curious if there's anything else you've seen succeed in allowing the best and most innovative brains to just do their thing. I know part of it is probably hiring amazing people. But yeah, is there anything else that's an escape hatch of just like, "Oh yeah, this person, just go. Go figure this out."
turns.zh: 我很好奇你是否还见过其他任何东西可以成功地让最优秀、最具创新性的大脑去做他们的事情。我知道其中一部分可能是雇佣优秀的人才。但是，是的，有没有其他什么可以作为逃生口，就像“哦，是的，这个人，走吧。去解决这个问题。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: To me, the unlock for organizations is managers, for this. Because you need managers to both detect the high performers and be like, "This person doesn't need the process." And then you need managers to give that person air cover to be like, "We're honestly..." Because what you're doing is, you're giving them some special treatment and you need to be kind of okay with that.
turns.zh: 对我来说，组织的解锁是管理者。因为你需要管理者既能发现高绩效者，又能说：“这个人不需要这个流程。”然后你需要管理者给那个人提供空中掩护，就像是，“我们说实话......”因为你正在做的是，你正在给他们一些特殊待遇，你需要对此表示同意。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And you also need to be okay with the organizational cost for that. Claire, who used to be the COO of Stripe, would always say, "Are you willing to break the org for this person?" And I always thought that was a really nice framing. And you kind of need to decide who you want to do it for, too.
turns.zh: 而且您还需要接受为此的组织成本。曾经担任 Stripe 首席运营官的 Claire 总是会说：“你愿意为了这个人而打破这个组织吗？”我一直认为这是一个非常好的框架。而且你还需要决定你想为谁做这件事。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But yeah, some people are just that good that like, "Yeah, of course you'll break the org for them." They're going to break the org in the best way possible.
turns.zh: 但是，是的，有些人就是那么优秀，就像，“是的，当然你会为他们打破组织。”他们将以尽可能最好的方式破坏这个组织。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I love that term. I think Claire's coming on this podcast. She just wrote a book, right? Is that the same person?
turns.zh: 是的。我喜欢这个词。我想克莱尔会来参加这个播客。她刚刚写了一本书，对吗？这是同一个人吗？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great.
turns.zh: 好的，太好了。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, she just wrote a book. Yep.
turns.zh: 是的，她刚刚写了一本书。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right, we just booked her. Come, and maybe we'll spend some time together.
turns.zh: 好吧，我们刚刚预订了她。来吧，也许我们会花一些时间在一起。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any other product building philosophies that you found especially useful in your time at Stripe, and Retool, and anywhere else?
turns.zh: 在您在 Stripe、Retool 和其他地方工作期间，您是否还有其他特别有用的产品构建理念？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I have a couple of, I guess, specific mental models that I use. The first is, build for your best user, not your worst user.
turns.zh: 我想，我使用了一些特定的心理模型。首先，为最好的用户而不是最差的用户构建。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And what I mean by that is, I think it's actually really easy to get stuck, or to focus on, "What if there's abuse of this product?" Or think about all the ways in which the product won't be used well. And then you end up sort of shaping the product in these really weird funky ways to make up for that.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我认为实际上很容易陷入困境，或者专注于“如果该产品被滥用怎么办？”或者想想产品在哪些方面不会得到很好的使用。然后你最终会用这些非常奇怪的时髦方式来塑造产品来弥补这一点。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Whereas in reality, the worst users, they should be a fraction of your users anyway. So you shouldn't really be building for them.
turns.zh: 而实际上，最差的用户无论如何都应该是您用户的一小部分。所以你不应该真正为他们构建。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I think a really good example of this is onboarding processes. Where, you're probably going to be building an onboarding process, where you're trying to collect a lot of data. Or trying to figure out, "Hey, how do I help this user who maybe isn't well suited for my product to be successful?"
turns.zh: 我认为一个很好的例子就是入职流程。您可能会在其中构建一个入职流程，并尝试收集大量数据。或者试图弄清楚，“嘿，我如何帮助这个可能不太适合我的产品的用户取得成功？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Really, you should just be building an onboarding process for the user who's going to jump into your product and get it immediately.
turns.zh: 实际上，您应该为将要跳入您的产品并立即获取它的用户构建一个入职流程。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I was thinking about this actually just the other day. Because we were in this product review, and we were talking about this other new product that we're thinking of exploring.
turns.zh: 事实上，我前几天也在思考这个问题。因为我们在这个产品评论中，我们正在谈论我们正在考虑探索的另一个新产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: More products? It never ends.
turns.zh: 更多产品？它永远不会结束。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. And we're kind of going down this path of like, "Oh, well if this gets really big, there's going to be all this abuse of the product." And Anthony, our founder was like, "Wouldn't that be an amazing problem to have?" And we're like, "Yeah, that's a really good point."
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。我们会沿着这条路走下去，“哦，如果事情真的变得很大，就会出现对产品的滥用。”我们的创始人安东尼说：“这难道不是一个令人惊奇的问题吗？”我们会说，“是的，这是一个非常好的观点。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So we kind of put that on the back burner.
turns.zh: 所以我们把它放在次要位置。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an interesting approach, because usually you're trying to optimize a flow, get more people through it, which are the least good users.You're saying you found more success just focusing...
turns.zh: 这是一个有趣的方法，因为通常你会尝试优化流程，让更多的人通过它，而这些人是最不好的用户。你是说你发现更多的成功只是集中......

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is this more initially, focus on the users that will understand this, and be excited about it, and make that work really well. And then, over time, build on that?
turns.zh: 是不是一开始就关注那些能够理解这一点、对此感到兴奋的用户，并使之真正发挥作用。然后，随着时间的推移，在此基础上继续发展？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, totally. Yeah, sure. If you're going to look at the end, and you're trying to optimize, et cetera, absolutely. But in that sort of early product development stage, it's just not worth it to be too focused on that.
turns.zh: 是的，完全可以。是的，当然。如果你要看看最后，并且你正在尝试优化等等，绝对是这样。但在产品开发的早期阶段，过于关注这一点是不值得的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. Sweet.
turns.zh: 知道了。甜的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So, that's one. The other one, our head of design, Ryan, always kind of reminds us of is, build the scooter, not the axle.
turns.zh: 所以，那就是一个。另一位，我们的设计主管瑞安，总是提醒我们，建造踏板车，而不是车轴。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So if you're trying to build the minimum viable product for a car, don't build just the wheels and the axle, build the scooter first. And then from there, you build the bicycle, and the motorcycle, and then the car.
turns.zh: 因此，如果您想为汽车制造最小可行产品，请不要只制造车轮和车轴，而应首先制造踏板车。然后从那里开始制造自行车、摩托车，然后是汽车。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And it's always just such a good reminder. You always want to start building the whole thing. But really try and think about the slice that gets the customer to complete value on a smaller thing first.
turns.zh: 这总是一个很好的提醒。你总是想开始构建整个东西。但要真正尝试并思考如何让客户首先在较小的事情上实现价值。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So with Retool Mobile for example, there's just so much you could be building there. And we decided very specifically, "Hey, we're only going to build this for companies that have field workers and they would need to do inventory management."
turns.zh: 以 Retool Mobile 为例，您可以在那里构建很多东西。我们非常具体地决定，“嘿，我们只会为拥有现场工作人员并且需要进行库存管理的公司构建这个。”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And it's a very specific slice, but it helps get through from something that was actually viable, beginning to end.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常具体的部分，但它有助于从头到尾从实际可行的事情开始。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So it's an approach for MVPs, basically. Make something simple and functional, not just something barely... Not actually working, but getting you to some dream product eventually.
turns.zh: 知道了。所以这基本上是 MVP 的一种方法。做一些简单而实用的东西，而不仅仅是一些勉强的东西……虽然不是真正起作用，但最终会让你得到一些梦想的产品。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. And then the last one is this idea of 70/20/10 split investments. I really think that a lot of product management can sometimes be reduced to funnels and portfolios.
turns.zh: 是的。最后一个是 70/20/10 分割投资的想法。我真的认为很多产品管理有时可以简化为渠道和投资组合。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So the 70/20/10 investments model in my head is just like, 70% of your building time should really be going to your core product, that has product market fit. 20% of your time should be going to strategic initiatives that aren't core, but they're strategic to the company, that you know have to do them. And then, 10% of your time should be going towards bets.
turns.zh: 因此，我脑海中的 70/20/10 投资模型就像是，70% 的构建时间应该真正投入到适合产品市场的核心产品上。你应该将 20% 的时间用于非核心的战略计划，但它们对公司具有战略意义，你知道必须执行它们。然后，你应该将 10% 的时间用于投注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's actually exactly the same heuristic I've always used. One question there is, how do you think about maintenance and bugs within that?
turns.zh: 这实际上与我一直使用的启发式完全相同。有一个问题，您如何看待其中的维护和错误？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. To me, that falls squarely in the 70%. So yeah, core product, tech debt, sort of the maintenance mode type stuff. And core product, obviously you're also doing a bunch of new stuff there too.
turns.zh: 是的。对我来说，这个比例正好落在 70% 之内。是的，核心产品、技术债务、维护模式类型的东西。至于核心产品，显然你也在做一些新的东西。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But yeah, no more than 70% of your resources should be going there.
turns.zh: 但是，是的，不应该将超过 70% 的资源投入到那里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What did you say the 20% was?
turns.zh: 你说的20%是啥？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Strategic initiatives that aren't your core, but you just know, based on your strategy, you have to do these things.
turns.zh: 战略举措不是您的核心，但您只是知道，根据您的战略，您必须做这些事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So the way I break it up is, 20% is where I put bugs and maintenance. And then 10% was big, ambitious bets. So it was similar ratios, but different things go into the buckets.
turns.zh: 知道了。所以我将其分解的方式是，20% 是我放置错误和维护的地方。然后 10% 就是一个雄心勃勃的大赌注。所以这是相似的比率，但不同的东西被放入桶中。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But, let me ask a similar question. How do you, at Retool, and maybe even at Stripe, think about finding time to do maintenance and bugs? Do you build it into roadmaps? Do you set off time to just fix all the bugs? I know it's probably an evolution, and it goes back and forth. But, any thoughts?
turns.zh: 但是，让我问一个类似的问题。在 Retool，甚至在 Stripe，您如何考虑抽出时间进行维护和修复错误？你会把它纳入路线图吗？您是否会安排时间来修复所有错误？我知道这可能是一种演变，而且会来回变化。但是，有什么想法吗？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. This, I think, is really one of the trickiest parts of product management, in my mind.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为，在我看来，这确实是产品管理中最棘手的部分之一。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: We don't have a company-wide sort of process on this. It's pretty team specific. Some teams do Friday bug bashes. Other teams are just, as products roll out, will work on them as they go.
turns.zh: 我们在这方面没有全公司范围的流程。这是非常针对团队的。有些团队会在周五进行 bug 攻击。其他团队只是随着产品的推出而进行工作。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I was actually speaking to a product manager at a different company, who mentioned that they just spent the last 18 months doing just product polish and bugs. And I think they landed in a place where they had to do it, because they just had so much debt. But luckily, we're not there yet.
turns.zh: 实际上，我正在与另一家公司的一位产品经理交谈，他提到他们在过去的 18 个月里只是进行了产品打磨和 bug 修复。我认为他们已经到了必须这么做的地步，因为他们负债累累。但幸运的是，我们还没有到那一步。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Right now, we let most of the teams just kind of do it themselves and figure out what makes sense for them.
turns.zh: 现在，我们让大多数团队自己做，并找出对他们有意义的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Awesome. I wanted to go back to something that I've heard about Retool, that you all are really good at. Which is PM's being really close to customers. And I'm curious what you've done there, or what the team has done there, that it's been really effective?
turns.zh: 好的。惊人的。我想回到我听说过的关于 Retool 的事情，你们都非常擅长。这就是 PM 非常贴近客户。我很好奇你在那里做了什么，或者团队在那里做了什么，是否真的有效？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Well, I do think every good product team figures out how to get close to customers. But just based off of my observations from Retool, and what I've seen at other companies, there are a couple things that are more pronounced at Retool than I've seen in a lot of other places.
turns.zh: 嗯，我确实认为每个优秀的产品团队都知道如何接近客户。但根据我对 Retool 的观察以及我在其他公司看到的情况，有一些事情在 Retool 比我在其他很多地方看到的更加明显。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: The first is, we have a lot of PMs who used to be in customer-facing roles, at Retool. I obviously am a big fan of that. I think there's just nothing like really understanding the value of your product, at the moment where a customer actually has to put money down. And so, I really like that about PMs, who have had those conversations with customers and they really get it.
turns.zh: 首先，我们有很多产品经理曾经在 Retool 担任面向客户的角色。我显然是它的忠实粉丝。我认为，在客户真正需要付钱的那一刻，没有什么比真正理解你的产品的价值更好的了。所以，我真的很喜欢产品经理，他们与客户进行过这些对话，他们真的明白了。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Second is, because the retail product is so technical... And I do think this just depends on what product you have. Our PMs are really, very technical. Everyone has either a CS degree, or has done some sort of engineering in the past.
turns.zh: 其次，因为零售产品技术性很强……我确实认为这取决于您拥有的产品。我们的 PM 真的非常非常技术化。每个人要么拥有计算机科学学位，要么过去做过某种工程。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Third is, we use Slack very heavily to talk to our customers and interact with them. So at this point, I think we have hundreds of Slack channels with customers. Every time we're testing a new product, or a new customer who's somewhat large, comes online. We will work with them in Slack, to get there off-the-cuff feedback, just back and forth. It's really nice. We just have this direct line to them, which is awesome.
turns.zh: 第三，我们大量使用 Slack 与客户交谈并互动。所以目前，我认为我们与客户有数百个 Slack 渠道。每次我们测试一个新产品，或者一个规模较大的新客户都会上线。我们将在 Slack 中与他们合作，来回获得即兴反馈。真的很好。我们可以直接联系他们，这太棒了。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, the fourth thing we do is, we use Retool to build Retool. So our product roadmap lives in a Retool app. And the app that we use to have feature flags for particular features, is a Retool app. So PMs are just in the product all day long, every day. They're their own customers in a lot of ways, and that really helps as well.
turns.zh: 然后，我们做的第四件事是，我们使用 Retool 来构建 Retool。因此，我们的产品路线图位于 Retool 应用程序中。我们用来为特定功能设置功能标志的应用程序是 Retool 应用程序。所以产品经理每天都在关注产品。他们在很多方面都是自己的客户，这也确实有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I didn't know that. That is very cool. So you build a task management product using Retool?
turns.zh: 哇，我不知道。这非常酷。那么您使用 Retool 构建了一个任务管理产品？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Oh, yeah. Well, we built many... Basically, all of our internal tooling happens in Retool. Like, our PMs, all their team dashboards are in Retool. All of their task tracking is in Retool. Submitting linear requests or bug requests happens in Retool, and then goes to Linear. So yeah, it's how we run the company.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。嗯，我们构建了很多......基本上，我们所有的内部工具都发生在 Retool 中。就像我们的产品经理一样，他们所有的团队仪表板都在 Retool 中。他们所有的任务跟踪都在 Retool 中。提交线性请求或错误请求发生在 Retool 中，然后转到 Linear。是的，这就是我们运营公司的方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You haven't been able to replace Linear yet? That's cool. I'm a big fan of Linear.
turns.zh: 你还没能取代 Linear 吗？这很酷。我是 Linear 的忠实粉丝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, two more questions and then I'll let you go. One is around product growth. Which, I don't want to get too into. We've talked about it a bunch on this podcast.
turns.zh: 好吧，还有两个问题，然后我就让你走了。一是围绕产品增长。对此，我不想太投入。我们已经在这个播客上讨论过很多次了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But, it's interesting that Stripe was very product-led growth. It was just self-serve PMs, engineers, whoever, just started using it. It grew and became enterprisey down the road.
turns.zh: 但是，有趣的是，Stripe 的增长是由产品主导的。这只是自助产品经理、工程师等刚刚开始使用它的人。它不断成长并变得富有进取心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Retool, on the other hand, I think people think it's product-led growth. I imagine it's actually sales-led, mostly.
turns.zh: 另一方面，我认为人们认为重组是产品主导的增长。我想这实际上主要是由销售主导的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so, I'm just curious what you've learned about the difference between building product and leading product teams within a sales-led org, versus a product-led org.
turns.zh: 因此，我只是很好奇您对在销售主导的组织中与产品主导的组织中构建产品和领导产品团队之间的区别有何了解。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I have a couple of insights on that. One interesting insight is that, teams that have one always want the other.
turns.zh: 我对此有一些见解。一个有趣的见解是，拥有其中一种的团队总是想要另一种。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so true.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Whenever I talk to candidates, I feel like you can always tell what their company has, because they'll be asking a lot of questions about the opposite. If they're probably a growth company they'll be like, "Well, how are you guys thinking about Enterprise?"
turns.zh: 每当我与候选人交谈时，我觉得你总能说出他们公司的情况，因为他们会问很多相反的问题。如果他们可能是一家成长型公司，他们会说：“那么，你们对 Enterprise 有何看法？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then, if they are more of a sales-led growth company, they're like, "Well, how are you guys thinking about your self-serve motion, or your product-led growth?"
turns.zh: 然后，如果他们更像是一家以销售为主导的增长型公司，他们会说，“好吧，你们如何看待你们的自助行动，或者你们以产品为主导的增长？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And my main takeaway, just in... And I don't know if I would even use the dichotomy of product-led growth, or sales-led growth, with Retool. I think we do have a lot of product-led growth. But we work with a lot of enterprise customers, and a lot of our revenue comes from enterprise customers, and we have a fantastic sales team.
turns.zh: 我的主要收获是……我不知道我是否会在 Retool 中使用产品主导型增长或销售主导型增长的二分法。我认为我们确实有很多产品主导的增长。但我们与很多企业客户合作，我们的很多收入来自企业客户，而且我们拥有一支出色的销售团队。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think the main thing is that, you just have to really figure out your interaction mechanisms with sales. And that just has to be so, so tight.
turns.zh: 我认为最重要的是，你只需要真正弄清楚你与销售的互动机制。而且必须非常非常严格。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And it goes in both directions. There's obviously, how you get feedback from them, because they are so often on the front lines talking to customers. Moreso than product managers, even.
turns.zh: 它是双向的。显然，你如何从他们那里获得反馈，因为他们经常在第一线与客户交谈。甚至比产品经理还要重要。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But it also goes the other way. If you are going to ship something, or if you are going to put out a roadmap, like, "How do you make sure that the sales team has everything that they need..." The sales, and in Retool's case, the success team and the support team, "Has everything they need to accurately talk to customers about that?"
turns.zh: 但也有相反的情况。如果你要交付一些东西，或者你要制定一个路线图，比如，“你如何确保销售团队拥有他们需要的一切......”销售人员，以及在 Retool 的案例中，成功团队和支持团队，“他们拥有与客户准确交谈所需的一切吗？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I've always actually found that really hard, because it's really hard to figure out the right altitude. If you're giving a presentation on the roadmap, people are either going to feel like it's too high level. Or, it's too low level for folks who maybe are new.
turns.zh: 事实上我一直发现这真的很难，因为很难确定正确的高度。如果您要就路线图进行演示，人们要么会觉得级别太高。或者，对于新人来说，它的水平太低了。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So this year, we're actually trying something different. We are doing a science fair. Where, each product team has a little booth. And they get to stand there, and anyone who has questions about the product can come... You know, from the go-to-market side, can come and ask questions, and get demos, and go as deep as they need to.
turns.zh: 所以今年，我们实际上正在尝试一些不同的东西。我们正在举办一个科学博览会。在那里，每个产品团队都有一个小展位。他们站在那里，任何对产品有疑问的人都可以来……你知道，从进入市场的角度来看，可以过来提出问题，获得演示，并根据需要进行深入研究。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So, I'll let you know how that goes. But I'm excited to experiment with it.
turns.zh: 那么，我会让你知道事情进展如何。但我很高兴能尝试它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Are there going to be foam core boards, and will there be ribbons?
turns.zh: 好的。是否会有泡沫芯板，是否会有丝带？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: There may be prizes. Who knows?
turns.zh: 可能会有奖品。谁知道？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. I can't wait to see a picture of this. Final topic. You have this concept that you call the product talent portfolio. What does that mean, and how have you found that useful in your product leadership life?
turns.zh: 我的天啊。我迫不及待地想看这张照片。最后的话题。您有一个称为产品人才组合的概念。这意味着什么？您认为这对您的产品领导生涯有何用处？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, it's back to like, all of product management is portfolios and funnels.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，一切又回到了原来的样子，所有的产品管理都是投资组合和渠道。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I think it's really tempting as a manager, to build a team in your image, because you understand their skillsets and you value those skillsets. And you're going to be able to detect and assess those skillsets better.
turns.zh: 我认为作为一名经理，按照你的形象建立一支团队确实很诱人，因为你了解他们的技能并且重视这些技能。您将能够更好地发现和评估这些技能。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: But the best product teams, in my mind, have really figured out how to balance the talent portfolio. So instead of having a bunch of PMs who all spike in one particular area, figure out how you can create complimentary skillsets for the whole PM team, so the whole is much stronger.
turns.zh: 但在我看来，最好的产品团队确实知道如何平衡人才组合。因此，不要让一堆 PM 都在某个特定领域发挥作用，而是要弄清楚如何为整个 PM 团队创建互补的技能组合，这样整体就会变得更强大。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And one way in which I like to do that is, I really like to balance product teams with homegrown product managers, who really get the product. They've probably been in it. They're amazing culture carriers, often. They really set the tone. But they may not have seen product management at other companies, and they may not have some of the more conventional and traditional product management skillsets.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样做的一种方式是，我真的很喜欢平衡产品团队与真正了解产品的本土产品经理。他们很可能已经参与其中。他们往往是令人惊叹的文化载体。他们确实定下了基调。但他们可能没有在其他公司见过产品管理，也可能不具备一些更传统的产品管理技能。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So I want to balance that with product managers who've come from other companies, and have done it, and can bring a little bit more of that product manager rigor. Even though they don't have, in the Retool case, the core Retool product management vibe.
turns.zh: 因此，我想在这一点上与来自其他公司并做过这件事的产品经理进行平衡，并且可以带来更多产品经理的严谨性。尽管在 Retool 案例中他们没有核心的 Retool 产品管理氛围。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: So, that's one example. I think there's others as well. Some PMs are just incredible execution machines. Other PMs are amazing visionaries. You kind of want a little bit of all of them.
turns.zh: 这就是一个例子。我认为还有其他人。有些产品经理就是令人难以置信的执行机器。其他项目经理都是令人惊叹的梦想家。你有点想要所有这些。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And you want to also balance within all of your different pillars. So we have three different sort of product pillars at Retool, and there's leads for all those pillars. And I always push the leads to hire people who don't look like them, so that we have balance everywhere.
turns.zh: 而且您还希望在所有不同的支柱内保持平衡。因此，我们在 Retool 拥有三种不同类型的产品支柱，并且所有这些支柱都有潜在客户。我总是推动领导雇用那些看起来不像他们的人，这样我们就可以在各处保持平衡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Do you, actively, as you're hiring, "Hey, well you're strong in these areas. Here's the person we need, here. We want this specific, super strategy minded person." Is that actually how you think about this?
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。当你在招聘时，你是否会主动说：“嘿，你在这些领域很强大。这就是我们需要的人。我们需要这个具体的、具有超级战略头脑的人。”您实际上是这么想的吗？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. I do a little personal exercise for myself every six months, where I chart out the team that we have today, and write down all of the strengths that we have, all of the weaknesses that we have, as a team. And then I try to hire specifically for those weaknesses.
turns.zh: 是的。我每六个月为自己做一次个人练习，列出我们今天拥有的团队，并写下我们作为一个团队拥有的所有优势和所有弱点。然后我会尝试专门针对这些弱点进行招聘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Any last pieces of wisdom or thoughts, before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 惊人的。在我们开始激动人心的闪电回合之前，您还有最后的智慧或想法吗？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I think that's it on my end.
turns.zh: 我想这就是我的结局了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. We got through everything I was hoping to get through.
turns.zh: 好的。我们经历了我希望经历的一切。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got six questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 至此，我们进入了非常激动人心的闪电回合。我有六个问题要问你。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you recommend most, to other people?
turns.zh: 您最向其他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Bird by Bird: Instructions on Writing and Life by Anne Lamott. It's incredible. So touching. Really, really great. Also, I think product managers should be great writers. So, I love that.
turns.zh: 一只鸟接着一只鸟：安妮·拉莫特的写作和生活说明。太不可思议了。太感人了。真的，真的很棒。另外，我认为产品经理应该是伟大的作家。所以，我喜欢这样。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And then the other book that I was going to say, but I'm glad you mentioned Claire, is Claire's book, Scaling People, which is coming out. I had a very small hand in ghost writing for her a little bit, in the first draft. So I use a lot of the early chapters from that book still, in management. And I still recommend the tactics in there, so I'm excited for her to get it out.
turns.zh: 然后我要说的另一本书是克莱尔的书《Scaling People》，即将出版，但我很高兴你提到了克莱尔。在初稿中，我为她代笔了一点点。因此，在管理方面，我仍然使用该书的许多早期章节。我仍然推荐其中的策略，所以我很高兴她能把它说出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I've been hearing about ghost writing as a career recently, and it feels like it could be an option for you down the road.
turns.zh: 哇。我最近听说代笔写作是一种职业，感觉这可能是你未来的一个选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to read the book. I haven't gotten a copy yet. I think you could pre-order it now, and we'll link to it in the show notes.
turns.zh: 我很高兴能读这本书。我还没有拿到副本。我想你现在就可以预订了，我们会在演出笔记中链接到它。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Nice.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's a favorite other podcast that you like to listen to, other than maybe the one you're on right now?
turns.zh: 除了您现在正在收听的播客之外，您最喜欢听的其他播客是什么？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah, this one's great. I can't choose between these two, though. One is Lex Fridman. And then the other is EconTalk by Russ Roberts. I really like that both of them are... Their agenda is curiosity, which I love.
turns.zh: 是的，这个很棒。但我无法在这两者之间做出选择。其中之一是莱克斯·弗里德曼。另一个是 Russ Roberts 的 EconTalk。我真的很喜欢他们俩......他们的议程是好奇心，我喜欢这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Totally resonate there. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've enjoyed?
turns.zh: 在那里完全引起共鸣。您最近最喜欢的电影或电视节目是什么？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Is it too basic to say White Lotus?
turns.zh: 说白莲花是不是太基础了？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. That's the most mentioned one, which says a lot, right? That just says how good that is, because I love it too. But, that works. Season one or season two?
turns.zh: 凉爽的。这是被提及最多的一个，说明了很多，对吧？这只能说明那有多好，因为我也喜欢它。但是，那是有效的。第一季还是第二季？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Oh, season two, all the way.
turns.zh: 哦，第二季，一路走好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, same. I'm excited for season three. No spoilers. Favorite interview question that you like to ask candidates?
turns.zh: 是的，一样。我对第三季感到很兴奋。没有剧透。您最喜欢问应聘者的面试问题？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: To what do you attribute your success? And you can't say luck.
turns.zh: 您将您的成功归功于什么？而且你不能说运气。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. Because most people look for, do they believe it's luck, versus their innate skill? So you don't even allow them to say luck? Interesting.
turns.zh: 有趣的。因为大多数人都在寻找，他们相信这是运气，还是他们与生俱来的技能？所以你连他们说运气都不允许？有趣的。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. Because I think humble people will always say luck in some way. And I always kind of wanted to know, "How self aware are you, and how curious are you?"
turns.zh: 是的。因为我认为谦虚的人总是会以某种方式说运气。我总是想知道，“你的自我意识有多强，你的好奇心有多强？”

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: And I think people who have really gone back and reflected on why are they where they are today, really says a lot about how they think about the world.
turns.zh: 我认为那些真正回过头来反思为什么他们会走到今天的人，确实说了很多他们对世界的看法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. What are some SaaS tools that you love, or use often, at your current company, or anywhere else?
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。您在当前公司或其他地方喜欢或经常使用哪些 SaaS 工具？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. Well, first and foremost, it's Retool. And then, the other SaaS tools that we use a lot, Slack, Gong, Linear and FullStory.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，首先也是最重要的，它是 Retool。然后是我们经常使用的其他 SaaS 工具，Slack、Gong、Linear 和 FullStory。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Favorite new product that you found, maybe in life, maybe at work?
turns.zh: 惊人的。您发现的最喜欢的新产品，也许是在生活中，也许是在工作中？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yeah. Have you heard of Rewind?
turns.zh: 是的。你听说过倒带吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, I have it running right now.
turns.zh: 是的，我现在正在运行它。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Nice. Yeah. I mean, I think it's really incredible what they've done.
turns.zh: 好的。是的。我的意思是，我认为他们所做的事情真的令人难以置信。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe describe it briefly, just so folks know what that is.
turns.zh: 也许可以简单描述一下，以便人们知道那是什么。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: It basically records everything that you're doing on your computer and then makes it really easy for you to search it. Which, it's just incredible. I don't know if you work this way, Lenny. But I feel like nowadays, I don't really go to tabs anymore. I kind of directly search for the thing that I'm searching for. And I think Rewind just fits that user behavior so, so well.
turns.zh: 它基本上记录了您在计算机上执行的所有操作，然后使您可以轻松搜索。这真是令人难以置信。我不知道你是否这样工作，莱尼。但我觉得现在我真的不再去标签了。我有点直接搜索我正在搜索的东西。我认为 Rewind 非常非常适合用户行为。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Eeke, this was so much fun. We got through everything I was hoping for, and more.
turns.zh: 惊人的。哎呀，这真是太有趣了。我们实现了我所希望的一切，甚至更多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out, learn more, see what you're up to? And, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 最后两个问题。如果人们想联系您、了解更多信息、了解您的动态，可以在哪里找到您？而且，听众如何对你有用？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Definitely find me online on Twitter. It's @EekeDM. And, how can they help us? Try out the Retool product and give us some feedback.
turns.zh: 当然可以在 Twitter 上找到我。这是@EekeDM。而且，他们可以如何帮助我们？试用 Retool 产品并向我们提供一些反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Retool.com, right?
turns.zh: 惊人的。 Retool.com，对吗？

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Thank you again, for being here.
turns.zh: 惊人的。再次感谢您来到这里。

turns.speaker: Eeke de Milliano
turns.en: Thanks, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you so much for listening. If you found this valuable, you can subscribe to the show on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app.
turns.zh: 非常感谢您的聆听。如果您发现这很有价值，您可以在 Apple Podcasts、Spotify 或您最喜欢的播客应用程序上订阅该节目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Also, please consider giving us a rating or leaving a review, as that really helps other listeners find the podcast. You can find all the past episodes or learn more about the show, at LennysPodcast.com. See you in the next episode.
turns.zh: 另外，请考虑给我们评分或留下评论，因为这确实有助于其他听众找到播客。您可以在 LennysPodcast.com 上找到所有过去的剧集或了解有关该节目的更多信息。下一集见。
